title: Why Does It Still Hurt?

verse.english: When their message came to him, Joseph wept.

readings.author: Sforno
readings.heading: The father he has lost
readings.text: When they recalled his father and his love, for [his father] had not suspected him.
readings.selection: Complete comment apart from the opening biblical lemma. Brackets clarify the pronoun. Working translation from Hebrew.

readings.author: Jonathan Sacks
readings.heading: Still afraid of him
readings.text: Yet still, all these years later, his brothers do not trust him and fear that he may still seek their harm.
readings.selection: One complete sentence from the published English essay. Sacks develops an interpretation he attributes to Rabbi Aharon Lichtenstein.

readings.author: Bereshit Rabbah
readings.heading: A missed invitation
readings.text: Rabbi Levi said that he no longer invited them to a meal. Rabbi Tanchuma said: His intention was only for the sake of Heaven. He said, “In the past, Father seated me above Judah, who is king, and Reuben, who is firstborn. Now it is not right for me to sit above them.” But they did not see it that way: “Perhaps Joseph hates us.”
readings.selection: First interpretation, from Rabbi Levi through the brothers’ suspicion. Opening biblical lemma omitted; separate pit interpretation not included. Working translation from Hebrew. Midrashic reconstruction, not a meal described in Genesis.

readings.author: Rabbeinu Bahya
readings.heading: Did he ever forgive?
readings.text: His brothers asked his forgiveness, but Scripture does not explain that he forgave them. … Although Scripture says, “He comforted them and spoke to their hearts,” which seems to indicate that Joseph was reconciled with them, we do not see Scripture mention Joseph’s forgiveness.
readings.selection: Selected argument from the first paragraph; omission marked. Bahya concludes that the brothers died without Joseph’s forgiveness. His subsequent account of punishment is outside the selection. Working translation from Hebrew.

questions: Why might Joseph cry even after choosing to care for his brothers?
How does the missed invitation change your reading of the brothers’ fear?
What would help you distinguish forgiveness from restored trust?

guiding_question: Can you forgive someone and still feel the hurt?

commentary.title: An apology is a beginning
commentary.label: READING THE SCENE
paragraphs: You accepted the apology. Then a short reply brings the old hurt back. You thought you had moved past it. Why does something so small still matter?

Joseph has welcomed his brothers and provided for them. Yet after their father dies, they fear revenge and ask forgiveness. Joseph weeps. Sforno hears grief for a father who trusted him. Jonathan Sacks sees the pain of brothers who still do not.

The midrash imagines a missed invitation. Joseph changes the family meal out of respect for his brothers. They read the change as rejection. Old fear makes an innocent gesture frightening. This is the rabbis’ interpretation, not an event Genesis describes.

Rabbeinu Bahya concludes that Joseph never forgave them. Sacks understands Joseph as having made peace with them, yet unable to win their trust. Caring for someone, offering forgiveness, and feeling close again may be different things. I hear a patient lesson here: lingering hurt deserves attention, too.
Selichah means forgiveness. Here the brothers use sa na, “please forgive,” from nasa, to lift, carry, or forgive. It is a different Hebrew root.

related_teaching.label: A PRACTICE FROM JEWISH TRADITION
related_teaching.title: Say what still hurts
related_teaching.author: Maimonides
related_teaching.excerpt: When one person wrongs another, the injured person should not hate him and remain silent. … Rather, he is commanded to tell him: ‘Why did you do this to me?’
paragraphs: For an ordinary strain in a relationship you want to repair, try completing this sentence: “What I still need you to understand is…” Then name one action that would help trust return. Leave room to listen.

subtitle: Forgiveness and the slow return of trust.
